cards.prompt: Your club's site, `example.org`, needs two things: an address for its website, and a place for its email to go. Does [[DNS]] give one answer for the name, or several?

options.text: Several: one name can hold different answers for different jobs
One: each name has exactly one IP address, used for everything
options.nudge: Think back to your first lookup: example.com already came back with two addresses.

options.text: One: email doesn't use DNS, so only the website needs an answer
options.nudge: Email has to find its server too, and finding servers by name is exactly DNS's job.

options.text: One: email needs its own separate domain, registered on its own
options.nudge: Club email can use the same name: `hello@example.org`. Could one name hold more than one kind of answer?

cards.explanation: One name can hold **several** answers. Your first `nslookup` already showed two addresses for example.com, and a domain can also say where its email should go. The website and the mail server are often different machines, so each job gets its own answer.
cards.hint: Remember your first `nslookup`: how many addresses came back for one name?

cards.title: One name, many answers
cards.body:
DNS keeps each kind of answer in its own **record**:

- **A**: the website's [[IPv4]] address (an **AAAA** record holds its [[IPv6]] address).
- **CNAME**: an alias, meaning "look up this other name instead".
- **MX**: where the domain's **email** goes.

When you look something up, you ask for one kind of record.

cards.prompt: Match each record for example.com to the value it could hold.
cards.explanation: **A** holds an IPv4 address (dots) and **AAAA** an IPv6 address (colons). **CNAME** holds another *name* to look up instead: `www.example.com` is an alias for `example.com`. **MX** names the mail [[server]], here `mail.example.com`.
cards.hint: Look at the shape of each value: dots, colons, or a name. Of the two names, which one sounds like a place for email?
cards.nudge: Dots mean [[IPv4]] and colons mean [[IPv6]]. Of the two names, one is just the main domain and one is a mail server.

cards.prompt: You're setting up email for your club's website, `example.org`. The site already loads fine. What extra DNS record do you need so mail to `hello@example.org` can arrive?

options.text: An MX record naming the club's mail server
A second A record with the website's address again
options.nudge: The website's address is already there and the site works. Email needs a record that says where *mail* goes.

options.text: An AAAA record with an IPv6 address for the site
options.nudge: AAAA gives the website a second kind of address. Email needs its own record that names the mail server.

options.text: A CNAME record pointing example.org to another name
options.nudge: A CNAME just says "look up this other name instead". Which record says where a domain's email goes?

cards.explanation: An **MX** record tells other mail servers where to deliver email for example.org. The website and the mail server are often different machines, which is why email has a record of its own. A and AAAA give addresses for the site, and a CNAME points to another name.
cards.hint: Look back at the list: which record is about mail?

cards.prompt: Run `dig www.example.com` and look at the answer. There are two lines this time.
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal, with dig's output shortened to just the answer. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: Look up www.example.com and show the answer
commands.output:
;; ANSWER SECTION:
www.example.com.	1800	IN	CNAME	example.com.
example.com.		1800	IN	A	198.51.100.10

success.question: www.example.com is an alias for which name?

cards.explanation: The first line is a **CNAME** record: `www.example.com` is an alias for `example.com`. The [[resolver]] followed it and found example.com's **A** record on the second line, giving `198.51.100.10`.
cards.hint: Look at the first line of the answer, the one with `CNAME` in it. The name at the end of that line is what it points to.
cards.nudge: Check the line with `CNAME` in it, not the one with `A`. The alias target is the last thing on that line, not an address.

cards.prompt: Put the steps in order for a [[browser]] opening `www.example.com`.

items.label: Get a CNAME record: it's an alias for example.com
Look up the A record for example.com

cards.explanation: A CNAME doesn't contain an address, just another name. So the lookup continues with **example.com** until it reaches an **A** record with an actual address. Only then can the browser connect.
cards.hint: A CNAME holds a name, not an address. You can't connect until you've got a real address.
cards.nudge: Each look-up comes before its answer, and connecting needs an actual address. What does the alias make the lookup do next?

cards.prompt: A message says "Log in to your example.com account" and offers four links. Which one really belongs to **example.com**?

options.nudge: Look closely at every character. One of them isn't the letter it seems to be, which makes it a different domain.
It starts with the right words, but what does it end with? The right-hand end decides who owns it.
A hyphen makes a new name, and this one ends with a different domain. Read from the right.

cards.explanation:
Read from the right. `login.example.com` ends in **example.com**, so it's a [[subdomain]] that example.com's owner controls.

- `examp1e.com` uses the digit **1** instead of the letter **l**. It's a completely different domain that anyone could register.
- The other two end in **example.org**, so they belong to whoever owns example.org, whatever the start of the name says.

Scammers register lookalike names like these to trick people into typing their passwords. Always check the right-hand end of the name.
cards.hint: Check the right-hand end of each name, letter by letter. The owner of that end controls the whole name.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- One name can hold several **records**, one for each job.
- **A** gives an address, **CNAME** an alias, **MX** the mail server.
- `nslookup` and `dig` let you ask [[DNS]] questions yourself.
